skill.name: enact-hello-ruby
skill.description: Runs a small Ruby greeting example through Enact and returns a personalized hello message.
skill.summary: Generate a Ruby-powered greeting from a provided name.
skill.author: EnactProtocol

security_audit.summary: The static finding at SKILL.md lines 32-34 is a false positive because it is a Markdown usage example. No malicious intent or prompt injection was found, but the manifest command on line 23 should handle user input safely.

remediation.issue: User input is interpolated into the manifest command string.
remediation.suggestion: Pass name as a separated argument or escape it through the Enact runtime.

finding_verdicts.reason: SKILL.md lines 32-34 are a fenced Bash usage example, not Ruby shell backtick execution. The referenced text does not execute during skill operation.

semantic_findings.title: User Input Interpolated Into Command String
semantic_findings.description: SKILL.md line 23 defines a command that includes the name parameter directly. If executed through a shell, crafted input could alter the command.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The command string clearly includes user-controlled input. Exploitability depends on Enact runtime argument handling, which is not shown in the reviewed files.

content.value_statement: Developers need small examples to verify Enact tool execution. This skill runs a Ruby script that returns a personalized greeting and Ruby version output.
actual_capabilities: Accepts one name input for the greeting.
Runs a Ruby script in the configured container.
Demonstrates a minimal Enact skill manifest.
limitations: Does not validate names beyond the schema type.
Does not call external services or APIs.
Requires safe command handling before production use.

use_cases.title: Verify Enact Setup
use_cases.description: Run a small Ruby example to confirm the local Enact workflow works.

use_cases.title: Teach Skill Packaging
use_cases.description: Show how a Ruby script, schemas, and command fit together.

use_cases.title: Prototype Ruby Tools
use_cases.description: Use the greeting flow as a starting point for Ruby command tools.

prompt_templates.title: Basic Greeting
prompt_templates.prompt: Use enact-hello-ruby to greet Alice and summarize the returned greeting.

prompt_templates.title: Default Input Check
prompt_templates.prompt: Run enact-hello-ruby without a custom name and describe the default behavior.

prompt_templates.title: Runtime Verification
prompt_templates.prompt: Use enact-hello-ruby with the name Morgan and report the greeting and Ruby version.

prompt_templates.title: Packaging Review
prompt_templates.prompt: Review enact-hello-ruby as a minimal Enact Ruby skill and list changes needed for production use.

output_examples.output: A greeting for Alice, followed by the Ruby runtime version.
A default hello message and the Ruby version used by the container.

best_practices: Use simple names when testing the example.
Review command interpolation before accepting untrusted input.
Treat this as a learning sample, not a production workflow.
anti_patterns: Do not pass secrets as the name value.
Do not expose this command to untrusted users without validation.
Do not assume the sample includes production error handling.

faq.question: What does this skill do?
faq.answer: It runs a Ruby script that prints a personalized greeting and the Ruby runtime version.

faq.question: Which tools can use it?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does it connect to the internet?
faq.answer: No evidence found of network access in the reviewed files.

faq.question: Is it ready for production use?
faq.answer: Review command argument handling before production use.

faq.question: What input does it accept?
faq.answer: It accepts one string value named name, with World as the default.

faq.question: Can it be extended?
faq.answer: Yes. It is a minimal Ruby example for building richer command tools.
